content: The term aphorism originates from the Greek word meaning distinction or definition. It refers to an original thought, expressed in a concise and memorable form, either spoken or written. The term was first used in the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, a collection of succinct statements about medical practice and human life. Over time, the term expanded to include pithy statements in physical sciences, philosophy, morality, and literature. Hippocrates' Aphorisms were the earliest known collection of such statements. Among them is the famous phrase: Life is short, art is long, opportunity fleeting, experimentation perilous, reasoning difficult: it is necessary not only to do what is right oneself but also to be supported by the patient, by those who attend him, and by external circumstances. This genre of writing evolved alongside literacy and became more prominent with the advent of printing, leading to the publication of aphoristic collections in book form. One of the earliest notable collections was Adagia by Erasmus of Rotterdam. Other significant early aphorists include François de La Rochefoucauld and Blaise Pascal. In the 20th century, influential collections of aphorisms included The Uncombed Thoughts by Stanisław Jerzy Lec (written in Polish) and Itch of Wisdom by Mikhail Turovsky (written in Russian). Aphorisms are typically concise statements that convey personal truths or observations in a clever and impactful manner. They can be poetic or prosaic, often employing literary devices such as repetition, parallel grammatical structures, or rhyme. For example: Lost time is never found again. — Benjamin Franklin Greed is a permanent slavery. — Ali Render unto Caesar what is Caesar's. Render unto God what is God's. — Jesus Christ Mediocrity is forgiven more easily than talent. — Emil Krotky Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm. — Ralph Waldo Emerson Death with dignity is better than life with humiliation. — Husayn ibn Ali That which does not destroy us makes us stronger. — Friedrich Nietzsche If you see the teeth of the lion, do not think that the lion is smiling at you. — Al-Mutanabbi When your legs get weaker, time starts running faster. — Mikhail Turovsky Many of those who tried to enlighten were hanged from the lampposts. — Stanisław Jerzy Lec A mystic hangs a fig leaf on a eunuch. — Stanisław Jerzy Lec The psychology of committees is a special case of the psychology of mobs. — Celia Green It is not uncommon to commiserate with a stranger's misfortune, but it takes a really fine nature to appreciate a friend's success. — Oscar Wilde Hypocrisy is the tribute that vice pays to virtue. — Attributed to François de La Rochefoucauld or a French proverb One death is a tragedy; a million is a statistic. — Joseph Stalin Believe nothing you hear, and only half of what you see. — Mark Twain It is better to be hated for what one is than loved for what one is not. — André Gide A lie told often enough becomes the truth. — Vladimir Lenin Like a road in Autumn: Hardly is it swept clean before it is covered again with dead leaves. — Franz Kafka Love the sinner and hate the sin. — St. Augustine Aphoristic collections have been a significant part of the works of modern authors such as Friedrich Nietzsche, Franz Kafka, Karl Kraus, Thomas Szasz, Stanisław Jerzy Lec, Mikhail Turovsky, Celia Green, Robert A. Heinlein, Blaise Pascal, E.M. Cioran, and Oscar Wilde. The 1559 painting Netherlandish Proverbs by Pieter Brueghel the Elder visually represents Flemish aphorisms of the time. Aphorisms are often considered a compressed poetic genre. They frequently use devices like alliteration (e.g., penny wise, pound foolish), anaphora (e.g., a penny saved is a penny earned), and rhyme (e.g., a stitch in time saves nine). For instance, the aphorism Children should be seen and not heard is a masterpiece of oral-poetic art, employing repetition of consonants and a rhythmic structure reminiscent of ancient verse forms. In many cultures, the ability to produce aphorisms spontaneously is a marker of social status. Traditional sages or cultural heroes, such as the Seven Sages of Greece, Confucius, or King Solomon, are often credited with aphorisms. Misquoted or humorously altered aphorisms are also a source of entertainment, as seen in works of satire or sports commentary. An aphorist is someone who creates or collects aphorisms.
